title: Scripture bears intrinsic divinity notes a well-disposed mind perceives, as critics scent an author
pass_a_gloss: But besides those arguments by-which to-be-asserted is-able against a-denier Scripture's divinity, Scripture in itself has illustrious very notes and indications of-truth and of-divinity, by-which itself itself proves and commends to-a-mind well affected, and whose eye not is blinded by-prejudices and perverse affections: although therefrom means suited for disputing to-be-taken not are-able, or certainly not so valid and efficacious. For just-as to-some-art's excellent work, as for-example to-a-Virgilian poem, or to-Apelles' painting, inhere certain-things by-which its author it-betrays, and for-itself itself claims: And these openly certainly and clearly are-recognized, although the-unskilled to those not attends, nor therefrom easily arguments are-able to-be-drawn against a-denier: So to-sacred Scripture deeply impressed are of-the-divine spirit footprints, and of-heavenly origin marks, which those discern for-whom the-mind darkened not is, and who are of-divine things skilled, and therefrom concerning its divinity certain become: although ignorant and profane men those-things make-light-of, or altogether not notice. And certainly, if any are learned in more-humane letters, when some human book they-unroll, easily they-note in it a-genius and character certain by-which into of-its author knowledge they-are-led. By-which reason Critics genuine writings to-their authors assert, to-Aristotle for-example, or to-Cicero, but spurious and supposititious writings they-expunge, although often that which sagacious Critics note and recognize, scarcely they-are-able to-explain and demonstrate to-another who not is in these versed: Shall we-doubt Prophetic and Apostolic writings to-savor of-the-divine Spirit, and in-them to-inhere a-something which a-pious and learned man perceives, and by-which from human and Apocryphal writings he-distinguishes them; although that not could against a-disputant and resisting-one be-demonstrated?
pass_b_english: But besides those arguments by which Scripture's divinity can be asserted against a denier, Scripture has in itself very illustrious notes and indications of truth and divinity, by which it proves and commends itself to a mind well affected, whose eye is not blinded by prejudices and perverse affections — although means suited for disputing cannot be taken from them, or certainly not means so valid and efficacious. For just as there inhere in some excellent work of art — for example a Virgilian poem, or a painting of Apelles — certain things by which it betrays its author and claims itself for him; and these are recognized openly, certainly, and clearly, although the unskilled does not attend to them, nor can arguments easily be drawn from them against a denier: so deeply impressed on sacred Scripture are the footprints of the divine Spirit, and the marks of heavenly origin, which those discern whose mind is not darkened, and who are skilled in divine things, and who thereby become certain of its divinity — although ignorant and profane men make light of those things, or do not notice them at all. And certainly, if any are learned in humane letters, when they unroll some human book they easily note in it a certain genius and character by which they are led into knowledge of its author. By that reason critics assert genuine writings to their authors — to Aristotle, for example, or to Cicero — but expunge spurious and supposititious writings, although often what sagacious critics note and recognize they can scarcely explain and demonstrate to another who is not versed in these things. Shall we doubt that the Prophetic and Apostolic writings savor of the divine Spirit, and that there inheres in them a something which a pious and learned man perceives, and by which he distinguishes them from human and Apocryphal writings — although that could not be demonstrated against a disputant who resists?
source_text: XXXII. Sed praeter argumenta ista quibus asseri potest adversus negantem Scripturae divinitas, Scriptura in se habet illustres admodum notas et indicia veritatis et divinitatis, quibus ipsa se probat et commendat menti bene affectae, et cujus oculus non est occoecatus praejudiciis et perversis affectibus: quamvis inde media ad disputandum apta sumi non possint, aut certe non ita valida atque efficacia. Etenim quemadmodum artis alicujus eximio operi, ut ex. gr. poemati Virgiliano, aut Apellis tabulae, insunt quaedam quibus authorem suum prodit, et ipsi se vindicat: Et haec aperte certe et clare agnoscuntur, licet imperitus ad ista non advertat, nec inde facile possint argumenta duci adversus negantem: Ita Scripturae sacrae alte impressa sunt spiritus divini vestigia, et coelestis originis notae, quas cernunt illi quibus mens obtenebrata non est, et qui sunt rerum divinarum periti, atque inde de illius divinitate certi fiunt: etsi homines ignari et profani ista floccifaciant, aut omnino non animadvertant. Et certe, si qui sunt docti in litteris humanioribus, cum librum quempiam humanum evolvunt, facile notant in eo genium et characterem quendam quo in authoris ejus cognitionem ducuntur. Qua ratione Critici germana scripta suis asserunt authoribus, Aristoteli verbi causa, vel Ciceroni, scripta vero spuria et supposititia expungunt, quamvis saepe istud quod notant et agnoscunt Critici sagaces, vix possint explicare et demonstrare alteri qui non sit in hisce versatus: An dubitabimus scripta Prophetica et Apostolica redolere divinum Spiritum, et iis inesse τι quod percipiat vir pius et doctus, et quo a scriptis humanis et Apocryphis illa internoscat; quanquam istud non posset adversus disputantem et repugnantem demonstrari?
